Corpus simply means a body — a collected, organized whole made up of many parts. Think of it the way you'd think of the word "body" itself: just as a human body is a whole system made up of organs, bones, and tissue, a corpus is a whole collection made up of individual pieces.

The word is used in several different fields, each applying this same core idea in its own way.
1. In Language and Linguistics (Most Common Use)

This is where you'll encounter the word most often today.

A corpus is a large, organized collection of real-world texts or speech — gathered together so that language can be studied scientifically.

Imagine you wanted to understand how people actually use the English language. You wouldn't just guess or rely on your intuition. Instead, you'd gather millions of real examples — newspaper articles, novels, conversations, websites, academic papers — and study them. That massive, structured collection of real language is a corpus.

What goes into a corpus?

  • Written texts: books, news articles, emails, social media posts, legal documents
  • Spoken language: recorded conversations, interviews, speeches (transcribed into text)

What is a corpus used for?

  • Figuring out how common a word is
  • Understanding how a word is actually used in real sentences (not just how dictionaries say it should be used)
  • Discovering which words tend to appear together
  • Comparing how language changes over time or differs across regions
  • Training AI language models and machine translation systems

Example: The British National Corpus is a famous collection of about 100 million words of British English from the late 20th century. Researchers use it to answer questions like: "Is the word commence more formal than the word start?" By looking at thousands of real examples of both words in context, they can give a data-backed answer.

Key point: A corpus isn't just a random pile of texts. It's curated — carefully chosen and organized with a specific purpose in mind. That's what makes it a scholarly tool rather than just a library.

In legal language, a corpus refers to the main body or substance of something — the actual, tangible thing at the heart of a legal matter.

  • The corpus of an estate is the total property, money, and assets that make up that estate (as opposed to the income it earns).
  • The corpus of a trust is the original principal — the actual sum of money or assets placed in the trust — as distinct from any interest or earnings generated from it.

You may also have heard the phrase habeas corpus — a Latin legal term meaning "you shall have the body." It refers to a fundamental legal right that protects individuals from being imprisoned without cause. The "corpus" here refers to the physical body of the person being detained.

In science, corpus is used to name a distinct body or mass within an organism — a part that is well-defined and functions as a unit.

Some common examples:

  • Corpus callosum: The thick band of nerve fibers that connects the left and right hemispheres of the brain. It's the bridge that allows the two halves to communicate.
  • Corpus luteum: A temporary structure in the ovary (formed after an egg is released) that produces hormones to support a possible pregnancy.
  • Corpus spongiosum, corpus cavernosum: Cylindrical bodies of spongy tissue in anatomy.

In each case, the word corpus is used precisely because these are distinct, organized bodies of tissue with their own identity and function — not just random tissue.

Outside of technical fields, corpus can refer to the complete body of work produced by a particular person, within a particular subject, or from a particular period.

  • "The corpus of Shakespeare's plays" — everything Shakespeare wrote, taken together as a whole.
  • "The entire corpus of ancient Greek philosophy" — all the philosophical texts that have survived from ancient Greece.
  • "Her corpus of research on climate change" — the full collection of her scientific work on that topic.

Here, the word carries a sense of completeness and authority — a corpus isn't just a few scattered pieces; it represents the full, recognized body of work in that area.

The plural of corpus is corpora (the classical Latin plural) — though corpuses is also widely accepted in everyday English. In academic and scientific writing, corpora is strongly preferred.

  • "Several corpora were analyzed to reach this conclusion."
  • "Linguists have built corpora covering dozens of languages."

No matter which field you encounter it in, corpus always carries the same underlying meaning: a body — a distinct, organized, unified collection or mass.

FieldWhat the "body" is
  • In linguistics: a body of real texts collected for language study
  • In law: the main body/substance of an estate, trust, or a person's physical body in legal proceedings
  • In biology: a distinct body of tissue within an organism
  • In general use: the complete body of someone's work or all texts on a subject

The connecting thread is always the same: many individual parts brought together into one organized, purposeful whole — a body.
